en.statement: Terraform configuration files list the step-by-step procedure Terraform uses to build infrastructure.
en.explanation: Terraform configuration is declarative: it describes the desired end state of the infrastructure, and Terraform works out the steps needed to reach it.

en.statement: Teams use Terraform to create a test environment on demand and destroy it once testing is done.
en.explanation: Codified infrastructure lets teams spin up development, test or QA environments when needed and decommission them afterwards, which costs less than keeping each one running.

en.statement: Terraform can manage cloud and on-premises resources in the same configuration.
en.explanation: Terraform's configuration language can describe both kinds of resources through their respective providers.

en.statement: HCP Terraform is required to manage resources across multiple cloud providers.
en.explanation: Terraform CLI configurations can use providers for multiple clouds; HCP Terraform is an optional hosted workflow.

en.statement: Terraform providers model SaaS features and DNS entries as resources, alongside compute and networking.
en.explanation: Terraform manages low-level components such as compute, storage and networking as well as high-level components such as DNS entries and SaaS features.

en.statement: Terraform converts configuration into each cloud's native template format and submits it for deployment.
en.explanation: Terraform providers call each platform's APIs directly to create and manage resources, so no cloud-native template service is involved.

en.statement: Terraform gives different providers the same resource schema for similar services.
en.explanation: Each provider defines its own resource types and arguments; Terraform supplies a common configuration workflow.

en.statement: Terraform uses one workflow to coordinate dependencies across cloud providers.
en.explanation: A multi-cloud configuration can express cross-cloud dependencies, which Terraform orders in one plan and apply workflow.

en.statement: Terraform forgets the resources it created once the apply that created them has finished.
en.explanation: Terraform keeps track of real infrastructure in a state file across runs and manages each resource throughout its lifecycle, planning later updates and deletion from the same configuration.

en.statement: Terraform picks one version of each provider that meets the version constraints of every module.
en.explanation: Each module declares provider version constraints in required_providers, and Terraform picks a single version per provider that all of those modules accept.

en.statement: Terraform expects a child module to reuse its parent's local name for a provider with the same source address.
en.explanation: Local names are module-specific: each module picks its own name in required_providers, while the source address is the provider's global identifier.

en.statement: Terraform verifies installed provider packages against lock-file checksums.
en.explanation: Recorded checksums let Terraform reject a provider package that differs from the selected dependency.

en.statement: The dependency lock file can record selected versions of remote modules.
en.explanation: The dependency lock file tracks provider selections, while module version constraints govern remote module selection.

en.statement: A resource that omits the provider argument gets its provider from the first word of its type.
en.explanation: A resource of type example_thing with no provider meta-argument maps to the provider whose local name is example in that module.

en.statement: An unqualified resource uses the first aliased provider configuration it finds.
en.explanation: A resource with no provider meta-argument uses the default configuration; if all blocks are aliased, Terraform implies an empty default.

en.statement: A resource's provider meta-argument can select an aliased provider configuration.
en.explanation: The resource can name a provider alias to use settings other than the default provider configuration.

en.statement: A child module inherits its parent's default provider configuration.
en.explanation: Default provider settings flow into a child module unless the module call supplies an explicit provider mapping.

en.statement: Terraform bundles provider plugins into each Terraform CLI release package.
en.explanation: Providers are distributed and versioned separately from Terraform, then installed for a configuration.

en.statement: Terraform state binds each managed resource instance to a remote object identity.
en.explanation: The binding lets Terraform identify which real object corresponds to a resource instance in configuration.

en.statement: Terraform can keep a clear mapping when two resource instances in state bind one remote object.
en.explanation: Terraform expects each remote object to be bound to one resource instance; binding it to several makes the mapping ambiguous and Terraform may behave unexpectedly.

en.statement: Terraform state retains dependency information after a resource block is removed.
en.explanation: The stored dependency metadata lets Terraform order destruction even when the removed block no longer describes its dependencies.

en.statement: Terraform state supplies the desired infrastructure configuration for a plan.
en.explanation: The configuration defines the desired state; Terraform compares it with state and live infrastructure to plan changes.

en.statement: Terraform state caches managed resource attributes to speed later operations.
en.explanation: Cached attributes can reduce the need for repeated remote API reads in workflows that use state as a performance aid.

en.statement: Terraform records in state which provider configuration last applied changes to each resource.
en.explanation: That record lets Terraform find the right provider configuration to destroy or refresh a resource after its block is removed from the configuration.

en.statement: Terraform discards data source attributes after a successful apply.
en.explanation: Terraform records data source results in state after apply, even though data blocks query rather than manage remote objects.

en.statement: Terraform stores ordinary root module output values in state.
en.explanation: Terraform evaluates an output's value and saves it in state so the root module can expose it after apply.

en.statement: Terraform falls back to resource tags to find remote objects missing from state.
en.explanation: Not every resource or cloud provider supports tags, so Terraform maps configuration to real objects through its own state rather than by tags.

en.statement: In the core Terraform team workflow, the team reviews a final plan after the merge, before apply.
en.explanation: Merge order or manual infrastructure changes since the pull request review can change the plan, so the team confirms the final plan before Terraform applies it.

en.statement: terraform init initializes the backend configured for the root module.
en.explanation: Initialization reads the root configuration's backend settings and prepares that backend for subsequent operations.

en.statement: terraform init can retrieve child modules named by module blocks.
en.explanation: Initialization fetches each referenced child module from the source named in its module block.

en.statement: terraform init provisions the resources declared in the working directory.
en.explanation: terraform init prepares the directory and installs dependencies; infrastructure changes occur during apply.

en.statement: Running terraform init again clears existing state before reinstalling providers.
en.explanation: Re-running terraform init is safe for existing configuration and state; it does not delete them.

en.statement: terraform validate errors in a fresh clone until terraform init installs the providers.
en.explanation: Validation needs an initialized working directory with the referenced plugins installed; terraform init -backend=false prepares one without touching the backend.

en.statement: terraform validate checks remote provider APIs for live resource errors.
en.explanation: terraform validate examines configuration structure; it does not validate remote services or provider APIs.

en.statement: terraform validate evaluates supplied input variable values for a run.
en.explanation: terraform validate checks configuration independently of supplied variables; terraform plan validates values in a run's context.

en.statement: By default, terraform fmt leaves files in subdirectories unformatted.
en.explanation: Without the -recursive flag, terraform fmt processes only the given or current directory, so nested module directories stay unformatted.

en.statement: terraform plan -target limits planning to the addressed resource instances and the objects they depend on.
en.explanation: Resource targeting narrows a plan to selected instances plus their dependencies; HashiCorp reserves it for exceptional cases such as recovering from mistakes.

en.statement: terraform apply with a saved plan file executes it instead of creating a new plan.
en.explanation: Passing a saved plan file to terraform apply runs the actions already recorded in that file.

en.statement: terraform apply asks for approval again when given a saved plan file.
en.explanation: Passing a saved plan file to terraform apply counts as approval, so Terraform executes it without another confirmation prompt.

en.statement: terraform apply -auto-approve skips plan creation before changing resources.
en.explanation: With no saved plan, terraform apply still creates a plan; -auto-approve skips the interactive confirmation.

en.statement: terraform destroy spares a state-tracked resource whose block was already removed from the configuration.
en.explanation: Destroy mode plans to delete every remote object recorded in state, including objects whose resource blocks were removed, and leaves an empty state.

en.statement: terraform destroy runs the same operation as terraform apply with the -destroy option.
en.explanation: terraform destroy runs apply in destroy mode and accepts most apply options; terraform plan -destroy previews the same deletions without carrying them out.

en.statement: Terraform resolves a dependency cycle by creating one resource first.
en.explanation: Terraform validates the dependency graph for cycles; a cycle prevents Terraform from deriving a valid execution order.

en.statement: Terraform can process independent dependency-graph nodes in parallel.
en.explanation: Terraform walks ready graph nodes concurrently after their dependencies have completed, subject to the parallelism limit.

en.statement: terraform plan -replace removes the selected resource from state before planning.
en.explanation: The -replace option changes the proposed action for an addressed instance to replacement; planning alone does not alter state.

en.statement: A resource block can combine count and for_each to create its instances.
en.explanation: count and for_each are mutually exclusive in one resource block; either argument can define its instances.

en.statement: A resource argument can reference an attribute fetched by a data block.
en.explanation: A data block reads provider data, and its exposed attributes can supply values to managed resource arguments.

en.statement: A data block can derive a provider query argument from a Terraform expression.
en.explanation: Data blocks support expressions, so query inputs can come from variables or other configuration values.

en.statement: Terraform can read a data source during plan when one query argument is unknown until apply.
en.explanation: Terraform defers a data-source read to apply when a query argument remains unknown during planning.

en.statement: A data source can be referenced in the type.label form of a managed resource.
en.explanation: Data source references start with the data. prefix, as in data.<TYPE>.<NAME>.<ATTRIBUTE>; the unprefixed <TYPE>.<NAME> form refers to a managed resource.

en.statement: Terraform can leave a computed resource attribute unknown until apply.
en.explanation: Terraform marks provider-computed attributes as unknown in a plan when their values emerge only after creation.

en.statement: terraform_remote_state exposes nested child module outputs as its own attributes.
en.explanation: terraform_remote_state exposes root module outputs; a child output needs an explicit root output passthrough.

en.statement: Two child modules can declare the same resource type and local label.
en.explanation: Resource addresses include the module path, so matching type-and-label pairs in different child modules identify different objects.

en.statement: A resource block's local label sets its remote object's name.
en.explanation: The local label forms Terraform's resource address and state identity; provider arguments control remote settings.

en.statement: Terraform prompts for a root input variable's value when that variable has a default.
en.explanation: A default supplies an input variable's value when the caller provides none, so Terraform does not prompt for that variable.

source.title: Use input variables to add module arguments

en.statement: Terraform can convert a numeric input into a string-typed variable value.
en.explanation: Terraform converts a compatible numeric value to text when an input variable has a string type constraint.

en.statement: Terraform rejects -var for a root input variable that is undeclared.
en.explanation: Assigning an undeclared variable with -var is an error, while an undeclared name in a variable definition file only triggers a warning.

source.title: Use input variables to add module arguments

en.statement: A TF_VAR_ environment variable can override a value supplied with -var.
en.explanation: -var and -var-file values take precedence over TF_VAR_ environment variables when they assign the same root input.

source.title: Use input variables to add module arguments

en.statement: A list(any) variable preserves mixed element types in the resulting list.
en.explanation: list(any) still resolves to one concrete element type; Terraform converts compatible values or rejects incompatible ones.

en.statement: A map(number) variable uses numeric keys to index its values.
en.explanation: In map(number), keys are strings and number constrains the entry values.

en.statement: Terraform discards extra attributes when converting a larger object to an object type constraint.
en.explanation: Object type conversion retains declared attributes and discards extra attributes from the supplied value.

en.statement: Terraform fills an omitted optional(string) object attribute with an empty string.
en.explanation: An omitted optional(string) attribute gets null unless the optional modifier supplies a different default.

en.statement: Converting a set of strings to a list orders the strings lexicographically.
en.explanation: Terraform orders string set elements lexicographically when converting the set to a list.

en.statement: A conditional expression can convert compatible result-arm types to a common type.
en.explanation: Terraform converts compatible conditional result values so the expression has one result type.

en.statement: A for expression inside square brackets returns an object keyed by input positions.
en.explanation: Square brackets around a for expression produce a tuple; curly braces produce an object.

en.statement: A for expression can filter input elements with an if clause.
en.explanation: An if clause in a for expression excludes source elements that fail its condition.

en.statement: A splat expression applied to a for_each resource reference collects one attribute from its instances.
en.explanation: Resources with for_each appear in expressions as a map of objects, so splat expressions do not work on them; a for expression collects the attribute instead.

en.statement: coalesce selects an empty string before later nonempty arguments.
en.explanation: coalesce skips null and empty strings, returning the first later argument with a usable value.

en.statement: try returns the first argument expression that evaluates successfully.
en.explanation: try evaluates argument expressions in order and returns the first result that raises no error.

en.statement: templatefile can read interpolation variables from the current module scope.
en.explanation: templatefile uses an explicit vars object to supply names referenced inside the template.

en.statement: can returns false when its argument has a dynamic evaluation error.
en.explanation: can turns a dynamic evaluation error into false, which is useful in input variable validation.

en.statement: A resource for_each expression can use keys computed during apply.
en.explanation: Resource for_each keys must be known before remote operations; keys that emerge during apply cause an error.

en.statement: Referencing another resource's attribute makes Terraform create that resource first.
en.explanation: Terraform treats references inside a resource block as implicit dependencies and uses them to order creation, updates and destruction.

en.statement: A depends_on on a module call delays just the child output used by the caller.
en.explanation: A module-level depends_on affects every resource and data source in the child module, not just one output.

en.statement: create_before_destroy forces replacement for a change that supports an in-place update.
en.explanation: The rule changes the order of a replacement Terraform already needs; it does not turn in-place updates into replacements.

en.statement: Terraform confines create_before_destroy to the resource declaring the lifecycle rule.
en.explanation: Terraform propagates create_before_destroy behavior to dependencies of the resource that declares it.

en.statement: With ignore_changes, Terraform leaves a listed argument unset when it creates the resource.
en.explanation: Terraform still uses ignored arguments when it plans a create; ignore_changes only suppresses differences when it plans later updates.

en.statement: Terraform checks a resource precondition separately for each count or for_each instance.
en.explanation: Preconditions run after count and for_each are evaluated, so each instance gets its own check and the condition can refer to each.key or count.index.

en.statement: A custom condition’s error_message requires a fixed string literal.
en.explanation: Terraform accepts any string-producing expression for error_message, including templates that include evaluated values.

en.statement: A failed check block reports a warning while Terraform continues its operation.
en.explanation: A check assertion can report an unmet condition without blocking the plan or apply operation.

en.statement: Terraform keeps an applied change in place when the resource's postcondition then fails.
en.explanation: A failed postcondition halts processing and blocks downstream actions that rely on the resource, but Terraform rolls back nothing it has already done.

en.statement: Setting sensitive = true on a variable block stops Terraform from writing its value to state.
en.explanation: The sensitive argument only redacts a value in CLI output and the HCP Terraform UI; Terraform still stores it in state and plan files.

source.title: Manage sensitive data in your configuration

en.statement: An ephemeral input variable can supply a value to a provider block.
en.explanation: Provider configuration is an allowed ephemeral context, so a runtime credential can avoid persistence in state and plan files.

en.statement: A root module output can forward a child module’s ephemeral output value.
en.explanation: Terraform permits ephemeral output blocks in child modules, while root module outputs cannot be ephemeral or expose an ephemeral value.

en.statement: When Terraform closes an ephemeral Vault secret, it ends the lease so Vault revokes the credentials at once.
en.explanation: Terraform opens an ephemeral resource when it needs the result, renews it if needed, then closes it; for a Vault secret, closing ends the lease.

en.statement: A managed resource’s write-only argument persists its input value in Terraform state.
en.explanation: Terraform passes a write-only value to the provider during a run, then omits that value from state and plan files.

source.title: Manage sensitive data in your configuration

en.statement: A provider determines which ephemeral resource types Terraform can declare in a configuration.
en.explanation: Terraform provides the ephemeral block syntax; the provider implements the available temporary resource types.

source.title: Manage sensitive data in your configuration

en.statement: Provider-specific credential environment variables require matching Terraform variable blocks.
en.explanation: Providers can read their supported environment variables directly; Terraform variable blocks are for Terraform input values.

en.statement: Running terraform output with -json redacts the values of outputs marked sensitive.
en.explanation: With -json or -raw, terraform output prints sensitive outputs in plain text; the sensitive argument redacts values in normal CLI output and the HCP Terraform UI.

source.title: Manage sensitive data in your configuration

en.statement: HashiCorp’s Terraform style guide advises keeping state files out of version control.
en.explanation: State can contain sensitive values; the style guide says to ignore state files and their backups in version control.

en.statement: A Git module source can target a subdirectory using // after the repository path.
en.explanation: The // segment selects a subdirectory inside the downloaded Git package.

en.statement: A module source from the public Terraform Registry uses a git:: repository address.
en.explanation: Public registry modules use a namespace/name/provider source address; git:: identifies a direct Git source.

en.statement: A module block can pass a resource attribute as an input to its child module.
en.explanation: Module inputs are arguments on the call, and Terraform can evaluate a resource reference as an input value.

en.statement: A parent module can read a child resource attribute through the child’s local resource address.
en.explanation: A child module exposes values through output blocks; the parent reads them as module.child.output.

en.statement: A root module’s input variable is available as var.name inside a child module.
en.explanation: Variables are scoped to their module. The parent passes a value through the module call to a variable declared by the child.

en.statement: Terraform downloads the newest registry release that meets a module's version constraint when none is installed.
en.explanation: Terraform first uses the newest installed version that meets the constraint; only when none qualifies does it download the newest acceptable release.

en.statement: In Terraform 1.12, a module call can build its source address from an input variable expression.
en.explanation: In Terraform 1.12 the module source argument takes a literal string with no template sequences or expressions; newer releases accept variables declared with const = true.

en.statement: A module block’s count creates child instances addressed with numeric indexes.
en.explanation: The count meta-argument gives each module instance an index, such as module.child[0].

en.statement: A module block's version argument selects the matching tag when the module source is a Git repository.
en.explanation: The version argument applies only to modules installed from a registry; a Git source picks a branch, tag or commit with the ref query parameter.

en.statement: Terraform selects the local backend and stores state on disk by default.
en.explanation: The local state file stays on the machine running Terraform, so other users do not share it by default.

en.statement: The local backend locks state through operating system APIs during writes.
en.explanation: The local backend uses system APIs to lock its local state file while Terraform performs write-capable operations.

en.statement: Terraform stops an operation that could write state when acquiring its lock fails.
en.explanation: Terraform halts the operation rather than continue with an unlocked state write that could conflict with another run.

en.statement: Terraform can lock state itself when the selected backend lacks locking support.
en.explanation: Locking is a backend feature: Terraform locks state only when the backend supports it, and each backend's documentation says whether it does.

en.statement: A backend block inside a child module changes where that child stores state.
en.explanation: A backend is configured for the root configuration. Child module resources share that configuration’s state.

en.statement: A backend block can use an input variable to choose its storage location.
en.explanation: Backend configuration cannot reference named values such as input variables; supply varying settings during initialization.

en.statement: terraform init can complete a partial backend configuration using an external settings file.
en.explanation: The file supplies backend arguments omitted from the root configuration during initialization.

en.statement: Terraform offers to migrate existing state after a backend configuration change.
en.explanation: Reinitialization after a backend change can copy the existing state into the new backend.

en.statement: A non-local backend writes a local state file after each successful Terraform operation.
en.explanation: Terraform normally handles state from non-local backends in memory and writes it locally only after an unrecoverable backend write failure.

en.statement: terraform apply -refresh-only writes refreshed values to state before the operator reviews them.
en.explanation: A refresh-only apply shows the changes Terraform detected and asks for confirmation before it updates state; the deprecated terraform refresh skipped that review.

en.statement: terraform apply -refresh-only restores remote objects to values in the Terraform configuration.
en.explanation: Refresh-only apply updates Terraform state and root outputs to reflect remote objects. It does not restore or otherwise change those objects.

en.statement: A moved block maps a resource's old state address to a new address during planning.
en.explanation: Terraform looks up the from address in state and treats it as the to address when planning, avoiding replacement caused solely by an address change.

en.statement: Renaming a module call with a moved block requires one mapping for each child resource.
en.explanation: One module-level moved block maps the old module address to the new one, including the address prefixes of its child resources.

en.statement: A removed block requires destroy = false to forget a resource and preserve its remote object.
en.explanation: A removed block normally destroys the object as it removes the state binding. Setting destroy = false preserves the object when the removal is applied.

en.statement: terraform state push accepts an older snapshot when the destination state has a higher serial.
en.explanation: Terraform rejects a state push when the destination serial is higher, protecting changes recorded after the snapshot being pushed.

en.statement: terraform state rm drops a resource binding immediately, before a later Terraform plan.
en.explanation: The command removes the binding directly from state and leaves the remote object intact. A later plan may propose creating a new object if configuration still declares it.

en.statement: Deleting an applied moved block from a shared module leaves its callers unaffected.
en.explanation: Callers still on the old address would plan to delete the object instead of moving it, so HashiCorp recommends keeping historical moved blocks in shared modules.

en.statement: A normal terraform plan may propose restoring a managed attribute changed outside Terraform.
en.explanation: Normal planning refreshes remote objects and proposes changes that bring them back into line with the configuration.

en.statement: terraform import binds an existing remote object to the Terraform resource address supplied on the CLI.
en.explanation: The CLI import command uses the given ID to find an existing object and records it at the supplied resource address in state.

en.statement: terraform import can write a matching resource block into the working directory after importing an object.
en.explanation: The terraform import CLI command updates state but does not generate configuration. Write the resource block separately for continued management.

en.statement: An import block lets terraform plan show the proposed import before terraform apply updates state.
en.explanation: Configuration-driven import appears in the plan, so you can review the target resource and any proposed changes before applying.

en.statement: An import block's to address requires a module prefix when it targets a child module resource.
en.explanation: Prefix the destination address with module.<name> to import into a resource declared by a child module.

en.statement: Leaving an import block in configuration after apply makes the next plan propose the same import again.
en.explanation: Import blocks are idempotent: once the object is in state at that address, later plans show no further import action, so the block can stay as a record.

en.statement: terraform state show can accept a module address and print attributes for its resources.
en.explanation: terraform state show requires an address for one resource instance and displays that instance’s state attributes.

en.statement: terraform show displays either the current state or the contents of a saved plan file.
en.explanation: The command renders state or a saved plan in human-readable form; giving a plan path selects the plan for inspection.

en.statement: Setting TF_LOG=INFO includes DEBUG-level Terraform diagnostic messages in the emitted logs.
en.explanation: Terraform log levels decrease in verbosity from TRACE to DEBUG to INFO. INFO omits DEBUG-level messages.

en.statement: Setting TF_LOG_PATH switches on Terraform logging and writes it to the named file.
en.explanation: TF_LOG_PATH only chooses where logs go; TF_LOG must also be set before Terraform writes any log output.

en.statement: An HCP Terraform workspace is a named state in the current Terraform CLI working directory.
en.explanation: An HCP Terraform workspace has its own configuration, variables, state, and runs in the hosted service. A CLI workspace is a separate state for one working directory.

en.statement: By default, an HCP Terraform remote run waits for approval between plan and apply.
en.explanation: HCP Terraform plans first and pauses before apply for approval in its default configuration. A workspace can also use auto-apply.

en.statement: A commit on a linked VCS branch can queue a run for an HCP Terraform workspace.
en.explanation: In the VCS workflow, HCP Terraform receives repository events and queues runs for changes to the branch linked to that workspace.

en.statement: A CLI-driven run reads its configuration from its HCP Terraform workspace's linked VCS branch.
en.explanation: CLI-driven runs upload configuration from the local working directory. A VCS-driven HCP Terraform workspace takes configuration from its linked repository.

en.statement: A Terraform cloud block belongs inside the backend block used for HCP Terraform state.
en.explanation: The cloud block is a direct child of the terraform block. It connects the configuration to HCP Terraform and is mutually exclusive with a backend block.

en.statement: terraform login obtains an API token for HCP Terraform through an interactive browser flow.
en.explanation: The command authenticates the CLI to HCP Terraform and stores the resulting token in local CLI credentials by default.

en.statement: An HCP Terraform workspace in Local execution mode passes its variables to local runs.
en.explanation: In Local execution mode, HCP Terraform evaluates neither workspace variables nor variable sets, so the operator provides variable values locally.

en.statement: HCP Terraform workspaces in the same project share remote state access by default.
en.explanation: New HCP Terraform workspaces do not grant peer workspaces state access by default; state sharing must be configured.

source.title: Manage workspace state in HCP Terraform

en.statement: An HCP Terraform workspace in Local execution mode still stores its state in HCP Terraform.
en.explanation: Local execution runs Terraform on the operator’s machine while HCP Terraform continues to store and synchronize the workspace state.

en.statement: Each HCP Terraform workspace belongs to a single project in its organization.
en.explanation: Projects group workspaces, and each HCP Terraform workspace belongs to exactly one project, including the Default Project.

en.statement: HCP Terraform separates workspace permission to queue plans from permission to apply them.
en.explanation: Plan access permits queuing plans; apply access permits approving and applying them. Teams can receive different workspace permission sets.

en.statement: A project-scoped variable set automatically applies to new HCP Terraform workspaces in its project.
en.explanation: Project-scoped variable sets automatically reach current and future HCP Terraform workspaces in the project, so new workspaces inherit the shared values.

en.statement: An HCP Terraform run trigger automatically queues a downstream HCP Terraform workspace after a successful source apply.
en.explanation: A successful apply in the source HCP Terraform workspace queues a new run in the connected downstream HCP Terraform workspace.

en.statement: An HCP Terraform policy set can target selected projects instead of the whole organization.
en.explanation: Policy sets can apply globally, to specific projects or HCP Terraform workspaces, or to workspaces with specific tags.

source.title: Manage policies and policy sets in HCP Terraform

en.statement: HCP Terraform gives OPA policies the same three enforcement levels that Sentinel policies have.
en.explanation: OPA policies in HCP Terraform have two enforcement levels, advisory and mandatory, while Sentinel policies have three: advisory, soft mandatory and hard mandatory.

source.title: Manage policies and policy sets in HCP Terraform

en.statement: The HCP Terraform private registry rejects provider packages published by an organization.
en.explanation: The private registry supports both Terraform modules and provider packages for organization members.

en.statement: HCP Terraform drift detection automatically applies the changes it proposes for a drifted workspace.
en.explanation: Health assessments detect drift and propose changes. An operator must queue and apply a run to restore the configured infrastructure.

en.statement: An HCP Terraform change request lets a team approve a pending infrastructure apply.
en.explanation: Change requests record workspace action items for teams. Run approval is a separate step in the Terraform run workflow.
